newsitem.title: USA: Higher prices loosen copper scrap, aluminum tight.
newsitem.headline: Higher prices loosen copper scrap, aluminum tight.

text.p: Copper scrap supplies in the United States appeared to be easing slightly as higher prices lure metal from reluctant merchants, traders said.
However, aluminum scrap was tightening as merchants held back in expectation of higher prices despite a potential strike in the key aluminum consuming automotive sector.
The Big Three auto makers are locked in labor contract talks.
Copper merchants said a key buyer of No2 scrap was more willing to pay higher prices which helped the market move up about two cents to 77 cents per pound.

"There seems to be an acceptable level of good material getting into the market place because of the higher copper prices," said Robert Stein of merchant Padnos. "But the spreads and discounts to COMEX are still very narrow."

Copper scrap prices tumbled since early summer following the crash in cathode prices due to the Sumitomo scandal. Some merchants were caught out with unhedged scrap stocks, having to buy in lower priced material to average down their inventory value.
Aluminum scrap prices have edged upwards because of the tightening market, but the big alloy makers have yet to push up benchmark LME deliverable A380 alloy prices.
Prices for A380 were still around 65 to 66 cents per pound, delivered U.S. Midwest, although some smelters were attempting to get 67 cents. Cash LME alloy settled Thursday at 56.78 cents per pound.
Alloy makers, diecasters and scrap merchants were all watching labor talks at the Big Three auto makers closely.

"Nobody is selling a lot of pounds, just truckloads. The scrap merchants are anticipating there will be no strike and prices will move higher," a Midwest alloy smelter official said. "On our customer base side they are buying, but buying cautiously and not building up inventory."
A Midwest aluminum scrap merchant added, "The guys don't want to sell. Everybody is anticipating higher prices."
The United Auto Workers have chosen Ford Motor Co as its target in bargaining with the Big Three. The labor contract at Ford expires on September 14.
A copper scrap exporter said No2 material for China was about 81 to 82 cents per pound fob west coast. Chinese business was stable but consumers were not able to get as much credit as they wished.
"For yellow brass, the market in India is too strong for the Chinese to compete," the exporter said.
